newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian arms plants struggle to survive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian arms plants struggle to survive.

text.p: Maps in the southern Russian city of Saratov do not mark its huge industrial graveyard. But as you drive into this pretty town on the River Volga you cannot miss it.

Right and left of the main road into town, in the northern district of Lenin, lie the remains of the huge weapon factories which, in communist times and with endless money from the state budget, gave work to about a third of the city.

The glory days are over. Since the end of the Soviet Union and the start of market reforms these companies are fighting for survival, trying to follow the biblical call to turn swords into ploughshares.

Those who eagerly started conversion, as the process of changing from military to civil production is called, have gone through bad times, often teetering on the edge of bankruptcy, and are disillusioned.
"CONVERSION EQUALS CONVULSION PLUS DIVERSION"
"We have a new saying: 'Conversion equals convulsion plus diversion'," says Yuri Tomnikov, the head of Tantal, which used to make radar systems for the Soviet army.
When President Boris Yeltsin and his reformers stopped subsidising their national armouries and ordered them to adapt to new times in 1992, Tantal felt the first of many shocks.
"At once our military production dropped enormously," Tomnikov told Reuters. From then on things went from bad to worse.
The company concentrated on producing microwave ovens and video-recorders, which it had started in the late 1980s. The result was disastrous.
The ovens and VCRs could not compete with the new foreign imports flowing into Russia and remained on the shelves.
"Our video-recorders were more expensive than those from Japan," said Tomnikov.
Their toasters faced the same fate. Their price was five times higher than that of imported ones.
Many Russian conversion plants have had similar experiences, unable to compete with imports in price and quality.
According to the State Statistics Committee, total production dropped in about 700 former military factories by some 26 percent in 1996. Civil production only increased in one plant out of five.
In 1994 Tantal became insolvent but reached agreement with its creditors to avoid bankruptcy.
Since then it has gone on a forced diet, changed its production lines again and realised that salvation lies in profitability.

In 1992 Tantal had nearly 20,000 workers, its own kindergartens, holiday homes and sports centres. These facilities are long gone, parts of the company have been sold and the work-force reduced to some 3,000.
Tomnikov is hopeful for the future of the 49-year-old firm. It now makes electronic cash-registers, automatic gas-heating systems and wants to start producing telephone exchanges.
But he says the politicians never really understood what conversion involved for the military plants.
"The programme was not well thought-out," he said.
SOME COMPANIES THINK STATE MONEY WILL SOLVE PROBLEMS
Politicians reply that plant managers have not yet adapted to a market economy.

Boris Shinchuk, responsible for economic policy in the Saratov region, some 900 km (560 miles) south of Moscow, said companies in transition do not co-operate enough with each other and still saw state money as the answer to their problems.

The manager of a conversion plant asked the regional government to buy him a production line, ignoring the fact that a company across the street had already got the very same equipment but was not even using it, Shinchuk told the Saratov newspaper Vesti.
"The biggest problem (facing the conversion companies) is excessive secrecy," he said.

Saratov, which as a centre of Soviet weapon production was the last of Russia's closed cities to open in 1992, is coping relatively well with an influx of job-hunters who have lost their work in the defence sector.
Thousands have found new jobs in small private shops and enterprises, the chemical industry or the Volga shipyards.
"Some trade at the market, or do odd jobs," said 30-year-old Misha, a scientist, who left a job in in the research institute of a military factory and now works in an advertising firm.
"I get by," he said. Not everyone is so lucky. Especially elderly scientists, the brains of former armouries, find it hard to make a new life.
"In the old times they went to their dachas, their country homes, to relax. Now they live off what they grow in the gardens there," said Yuri Alexandrovich, a 62-year-old physicist.
